title: Coding Agents for Teaching Economics
text:
Preface
This handbook is for people who teach economics and want to use a coding agent to prepare and run a module. It covers lecture material, problem sets and code labs, assessment design, marking, checking, and the rules that apply at UK universities.
The main text does not depend on a particular product. Notes headed In Claude Code give the specifics for that tool. Those notes, and the university policies cited, were checked on 26 November 2026 and will date.
The templates in the appendix are also files in the templates/ folder of the repository. None has been tested on a live module.
This is general guidance and not legal advice. Your own institution’s policy takes precedence.
Licence. Text and templates are released under CC BY-NC 4.0: you may reuse and adapt them for non-commercial purposes with attribution.

title: 1  Scope and how to use this handbook
text:
This handbook is for colleagues who teach economics and want to use a coding agent to prepare and run a module. It covers lecture material, problem sets and code labs, assessment design, marking, checking, and the rules that apply.
A coding agent is a language model that works inside a folder on your computer: it reads your files, writes new ones and runs code. Chapter 2 explains how that differs from a chat window. No programming is needed to follow the handbook, although chapter 5 is most useful for modules with a computational component.
Tool. The main text does not depend on a particular product. Where the mechanics matter, a short note headed In Claude Code gives the specifics. Those notes were checked against the Claude Code documentation on 26 November 2026 and will date faster than the rest.
Examples. Most worked examples come from quantitative finance and econometrics. Each section also says how the same workflow applies to macroeconomics, applied economics and economic theory, where the material is more often derivations, models and essays than code.
Policy. Chapters 6, 7, 9 and 10 describe the position at UK universities in general. Your own institution’s policy takes precedence, and several of the rules differ across universities.
What is left out. This is not a guide for students, and it does not cover research use. It does not compare products or discuss procurement.
Reading paths.

New to coding agents: chapters 2 and 3, then whichever of 4 to 7 matches the task in front of you.
Already using one: chapters 5 to 8, and the templates in the appendix.
Module or programme lead: chapters 6, 7, 9 and 10.
crumbs: 1  Scope and how to use this handbook

title: 2  What a coding agent is
text:
A coding agent works directly on the files in a folder, whereas a chat window works only on what is pasted or uploaded into the conversation. That one difference explains both why it is more useful for teaching preparation and why it needs more care.









Chat window
Coding agent




What it sees
What you paste or upload
Every file in the folder you open it in


What it produces
Text in the conversation
Files on disk: notes, slides, notebooks, spreadsheets


Running code
Limited or none
Runs what is installed on your machine (Python, R, Stata, LaTeX) and reads the result


Continuity
Depends on what you re-supply or what the product remembers
Reads a standing instruction file at the start of every session


Scale
One document at a time
A whole module, or a folder of scripts, in one task



What this changes in practice. You can ask for a problem set and its solutions, have the solutions executed, and get back the files with the numerical answers already checked. You can ask for the notation in ten weeks of slides to be made consistent. Neither is practical by copying and pasting.
What it does not change. The model still makes confident mistakes: a sign error in a derivation, a reference that does not exist, a question that is harder than intended. Running code catches numerical errors but not a wrong economic argument; chapter 8 covers checking.
Permissions. Because the agent can edit and delete files, every product has a setting for what it may do without asking. Three habits are enough to start:

Open the agent in a folder made for the module and never in your home folder.
Begin in the mode that asks before each edit, and relax it once you have seen how the agent behaves.
Keep the folder under version control or in a synced drive with file history, so any change can be undone.


In Claude Code. It runs in a terminal, a desktop app, VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and the browser (platforms). The desktop app is the easiest start for colleagues who do not use a terminal.
The permission modes are Manual (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits files in the folder without asking), plan (reads and proposes, changes nothing until you approve) and auto (acts without asking, with a separate model reviewing its actions). Recent versions start interactive terminal and VS Code sessions in auto, so switch to Manual or plan for a first session. In the terminal, Shift+Tab cycles through the modes.
crumbs: 2  What a coding agent is

title: 3  Setting up a module folder
text:
Each module needs one folder, with your source material separated from what the agent produces and one short instruction file at the top. The chapters that follow assume this setup.
Folder layout. The layout below works for most modules.
ECN000-module-name/
  MODULE.md            standing instructions (see below)
  sources/             your notes, papers, past slides, textbook references (read-only)
  lectures/            week01/, week02/, ... notes and slides
  problem-sets/        ps1/ questions, solutions, code, data
  assessment/          coursework briefs, exams, rubrics, marking schemes
  data/                datasets used in labs and coursework
  admin/               module outline, schedule, announcements
Keep sources/ read-only by convention: the agent reads from it and never edits it. Keep assessment/ out of any folder that is shared with students or synced to the virtual learning environment.
The module instruction file. This is the file the agent reads at the start of every session. It replaces the paragraph of context you would otherwise retype each time. It should hold:

Module facts: code, title, level, credits, cohort size, prerequisites.
Learning outcomes: as approved in the module specification.
What students already know: which mathematics, statistics and programming can be assumed, and what cannot.
Notation: your symbols for returns, expectations, estimators, vectors and matrices, and which textbook’s conventions you follow.
Software: language and version, permitted libraries, how code is run.
House style: slide template, length of a lecture, how worked examples are laid out, British spelling.
Rules: never invent a reference; never edit sources/; every numerical answer must come from code that has been run.
Decisions log: dated one-line notes on choices made, so they are not reopened next year.

Keep it to one or two pages. A long file is followed less reliably than a short one. Put detail that applies to one task, such as a marking rubric, in its own file and point to it.
Other fields. For a theory or macroeconomics module, the notation and assumed-mathematics entries matter most. For an applied or policy module, add the data sources you use and the standard of evidence you expect in written work.

In Claude Code. The instruction file is called CLAUDE.md and sits at the top of the folder. It is loaded at the start of every session, and the documentation recommends keeping it under 200 lines (memory). The /init command drafts one from the folder’s contents. A line such as @assessment/rubric.md imports another file.
Claude Code treats the file as context and does not enforce it, so the read-only convention for sources/ should also be set as a deny rule in the permission settings. Claude Code also reads a file named AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md is present, which helps if colleagues use different tools. Separately, it keeps its own notes on your corrections (auto memory); review them occasionally.
crumbs: 3  Setting up a module folder

title: 4  Lecture material from your own sources
text:
The agent is most reliable when it reorganises material you supply and least reliable when it writes from its own knowledge. Build lectures from your sources/ folder and treat anything it adds from outside as unverified.
A workflow that holds up.

Collect the sources. Put your notes, the papers and chapters the lecture draws on, and last year’s slides in sources/.
Ask for a plan before any writing. One page per lecture: the outcomes it serves, the sequence of ideas, the worked examples, what is cut. Edit the plan yourself. This is where your judgement about the cohort enters.
Write the notes first. Full lecture notes in prose and mathematics, from the approved plan.
Derive the slides from the notes. Slides are then a view of one source, and a later correction is made in one place.
Generate every figure from code. Keep the script next to the figure so it can be rerun with new data.
Run a consistency pass. Across all weeks: notation, numbering, cross-references, terms defined before use.

File formats. Plain-text formats work best because the agent can compile them and compare versions: LaTeX and Beamer, or Markdown with Quarto. It can also produce PowerPoint and Word files, but changes are harder to review.
An example request.
Read sources/week05/ and the plan in lectures/week05/plan.md.
Write lecture notes for week 5 (generalised method of moments) in LaTeX.
Use only the material in sources/. Follow the notation in MODULE.md.
If you need a result that is not in the sources, stop and list it; do not supply it.
Aim for what can be taught in 100 minutes, with two worked examples.
Compile the file and fix any errors before you finish.
What to watch.

Length. Agents write too much. State the teaching time and the number of examples.
Level. The agent has no information about what your students find hard. Say so in the plan: where to slow down, which step needs intuition before algebra.
Invented support. References, dates, numbers in a motivating example and attributed quotations all need checking against a source (chapter 8).
Flat prose. Material written from generic knowledge reads like a textbook summary. Your own notes give the module its character.

Updating a module year to year. Ask the agent to list what has dated: data ending in an old year, superseded references, examples overtaken by events. Rerun the figure scripts with current data. Review the changes as a comparison against last year’s files before accepting them.
By field.

Econometrics and quantitative finance: have every estimate, table and figure in the notes produced by a script in the folder, on data students can also access.
Macroeconomics: model derivations benefit from the independent re-derivation in chapter 8. Charts of UK or international data should be built from the official series by script, with the download date recorded.
Economic theory: ask for proofs with every step written out, then have them checked separately. Agents skip steps that look obvious and are sometimes wrong.
Applied and policy modules: case studies are where invented facts appear most often. Supply the documents and require a citation for each factual claim.


In Claude Code. Use plan mode for step 2: the agent reads the sources and proposes, and nothing is written until you approve. Once the workflow is settled, store it as a skill so that a new lecture is one command (chapter 11).
crumbs: 4  Lecture material from your own sources

title: 5  Problem sets, solutions and code labs
text:
No solution goes to students unless it has been produced by code that ran, or re-derived independently. This rule is the main safeguard for agent-written exercises, and it is the main advantage an agent has over a chat window.
Writing a problem set.

Specify before generating. The topic, the learning outcome each question tests, the number of questions, the intended time, and the mix of mechanical, applied and stretch questions.
Supply two or three of your own past questions as the standard for style and difficulty. Examples tend to calibrate the agent better than a written description.
Ask for questions and solutions as separate files, with the solution code in a third.
Have the solution code executed and the numbers in the written solutions taken from its output rather than typed by the model.
Have the questions solved again from scratch by a separate session that has not seen the solutions, and compare (chapter 8).
Attempt the stretch questions yourself. Agents often misjudge how hard a question is.

Example: an empirical finance question. Students estimate the CAPM beta of five stocks on monthly returns and test whether the alphas are jointly zero. The agent writes the question, a script that downloads or loads the data and runs the regressions, and a solution whose betas, standard errors and test statistic are read from the script’s output. If the data file changes next year, rerunning the script updates the solution.
Variants. Once a question is driven by a script, variants are cheap: change the seed, the sample period or the parameter values, rerun, and a new numerical answer follows. Variants are useful for tutorial groups, resits and individualised coursework. Keep the seed and parameters for each variant in a file so any version can be reproduced.
Code labs and notebooks.

Require that each notebook runs from top to bottom in a clean environment before it is released. Ask the agent to do exactly that and report failures.
Pin the software: language version and package versions in a file in the folder.
Produce the student version from the solution version by removing marked cells, so the two cannot drift apart.
Keep data small and included in the folder, or downloaded by a script with the date recorded.

Questions without code.

Derivations and proofs (theory, macro): the equivalent of running the code is a symbolic or numerical check. Ask the agent to verify a closed-form answer with a computer algebra system, or to confirm a comparative-statics sign numerically at several parameter values. Such a check catches algebra slips but not flawed arguments.
Short-answer and essay questions (applied, policy): ask for a marking scheme alongside each question, stating what a pass, merit and distinction answer contains. Writing the scheme exposes questions that are vague or have several defensible answers.

What to watch.

Questions that are answerable without the intended method.
Numbers chosen so that the answer is uninformative, such as a test statistic nowhere near the critical value.
Solutions that state a correct number with an incorrect interpretation.
Questions that closely reproduce a textbook exercise (chapter 9).


In Claude Code. The agent runs the scripts and notebooks itself and reads the output, so step 4 is one instruction: “take every number in the solutions from the script output”. For step 5, a subagent starts with a fresh context and can be instructed to read only the questions (subagents).
crumbs: 5  Problem sets, solutions and code labs

title: 6  Assessment design when students have the same tools
text:
Before setting any unsupervised assessment, give it to an agent yourself and mark what comes back. The result tells you what the assessment still measures, which is more useful than a general view on whether students “will use AI”.
The stress test.

Start a fresh session in an empty folder, with none of your module files.
Give the agent exactly what a student receives: the brief, the data, the reading list.
Ask it to complete the assessment in one pass, then once more with one round of the kind of follow-up a student would give (“make it more critical”, “check the code runs”).
Mark both outputs against your rubric, ideally mixed in with past student scripts and marked blind.
Record where it lost marks. Those are the parts of the assessment that still discriminate.

Repeat it each year. The answer changes as the tools improve, and a result from two years ago is not evidence about this year’s cohort.
Decide what must be shown unaided. Go through the learning outcomes and sort them into two groups: those a student must demonstrate without assistance, and those where using the tools well is part of the skill. The first group needs supervised conditions. The second can be assessed in coursework where AI use is permitted and the standard is raised accordingly.
Formats and what they still tell you.








Format
What it shows
Main cost




Invigilated written exam
Unaided knowledge and reasoning
Narrow range of skills; exam logistics


Invigilated computer exam, no network
Unaided coding and data work
Lab capacity; technical setup


Coursework plus short oral examination
Whether the student understands what they submitted
Staff time per student


Coursework with process evidence (drafts, version history, a log of AI use)
How the work was produced
Marking load; evidence can be manufactured


Coursework with AI permitted and assessed
Judgement: framing, verification, critique of output
Needs a rubric that rewards those things


In-class tasks and presentations
Performance in real time
Timetabling; anxiety for some students



Individualised data or parameters (chapter 5) deter copying between students. They do not make a task harder for an agent.
State the rule for each assessment. Students need to know, per assessment, what use is allowed. A published scale helps keep this consistent across a programme. The AI Assessment Scale of Perkins, Roe and Furze is one such scale, with five levels running from “No AI” to “AI Exploration”.
Sector position. The Russell Group principles commit member universities to adapting teaching and assessment, upholding academic integrity, and attempting fair access where tools sit behind a paywall. If an assessment permits or expects AI use, check that every student can use an adequate tool at no cost.
Detection software. UCL states that it is not investing in detection software and that staff must not submit student work to such tools.
Lead times. Changing the assessment type or weighting can require a module amendment, which at some universities must be approved months ahead. A stress test in the spring leaves time to change the following year’s assessment.
By field. Take-home problem sets and empirical projects with a standard dataset are the most exposed. Proof-based theory questions and essays on well-covered topics should not be assumed safe; test them the same way. Work that depends on material the agent cannot see, such as an in-class experiment, a local dataset the student collected or a seminar discussion, is less so.
crumbs: 6  Assessment design when students have the same tools

title: 7  Marking and feedback
text:
The lecturer reads the work and sets the mark; the agent can help with everything around that. This is the position in the university guidance cited below, and the evidence on machine marking supports it. Check your own institution’s rule before uploading any student work to any tool (chapter 9).
What the evidence says. Two recent UK studies of extended written work reach the same conclusion.

Kay, Rutherford, Smith, Shore and Francis (2026), in Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, find that language models gave higher marks than human markers with much less spread: weak essays were marked up and strong essays marked down.
Corsi et al. (2026) compare three models on 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities. Agreement with human marks varied widely by model, prompt and institution, all models pulled marks towards the middle, and averaging across models did not remove the problem.

Compression towards the middle matters for classification boundaries: if it carries over to UK degree marking, the scripts most at risk are the fails and the firsts. Results are better for short structured answers. A study of an introductory programming course reports exact agreement between a model and human graders on 80% of 6,345 answers. None of these studies covers economics or finance.
What universities allow. Rules differ, but published guidance shares a core.



Rule
Example




A human allocates the mark
York: marking is not delegated to AI, except questions with no academic judgement such as multiple choice


A subject expert reads every script
Exeter (September 2026)


Student work goes only into approved tools, or not at all
York requires explicit student permission; Exeter restricts it to licensed tools and requires students’ informed consent


Students are told when and how AI is used
York, Exeter


All markers on an assessment use the same approach
York, Exeter



A Loughborough review of staff guidance at 16 UK universities found that only a minority gave concrete direction on marking, moderation or feedback. If yours is silent, ask before proceeding.
Uses that stay inside these rules.

Rubric design. Draft and test a rubric against the learning outcomes before the assessment is set. No student work is involved.
Marking schemes for numerical work. Generate the scheme from the solution script, with method marks and common wrong answers.
Feedback from your notes. You read the script and write brief notes; the agent expands them into full sentences mapped to the rubric criteria. You approve the result.
Cohort-level feedback. Summarise the themes in your own comments across all scripts into a report for the class.
Automated checks on code. Run each submission’s code against tests you wrote. This is conventional autograding, and the agent’s role is to help write the tests.
Consistency checks. After marking, ask whether your comments and marks on a criterion are consistent across scripts. The agent sees your marks and comments, anonymised.

Uses to avoid.

Asking for a mark and adopting it.
Asking for a mark first and then reading the script. The suggested mark can anchor your judgement.
Uploading scripts with names or student numbers to a tool your university has not approved.
Sending feedback you have not read in full.

Where it is permitted and you want a second view. Mark first, record your mark, then compare. Treat a disagreement as a prompt to reread, in the same way as a second marker’s view, and keep the decision yours.

In Claude Code. Marking support works on files in a folder, so anonymise first: one file per script named by candidate number, with your notes alongside. Whether the tool may be used at all depends on the account type and your university’s approval (chapter 9).

title: 8  Checking the output
text:
Everything the agent produces is a draft until it has passed a check that does not rely on the session that wrote it. Students treat teaching material as correct, so an error in a solution or a slide costs more than an error in a draft paper.
Match the check to the kind of error.








Kind of error
Check
Who




Wrong number in a solution or table
Number is read from the output of code that ran
Agent


Code that fails on a student’s machine
Run from top to bottom in a clean environment with pinned versions
Agent


Algebra slip in a derivation
Symbolic or numerical verification of the result
Agent


Flawed step in a proof or argument
Independent re-derivation in a fresh session, then your own reading
Agent, then you


Reference that does not exist or does not say what is claimed
Each reference opened at its DOI or URL and the claim located in it
Agent, then you for key ones


Wrong fact, date or figure in an example
Traced to a document in sources/ or a cited official series
Agent


Inconsistent notation across weeks
Consistency pass against MODULE.md
Agent


Wrong level, emphasis or tone
Your reading
You



Why a fresh session. A session that has just written a solution may simply confirm it when asked to check. A second session that sees only the question has not seen the first answer. Where the two disagree, one of them is wrong, and that is where to spend your time.
An independent reviewer for all material. A second agent should review every piece of material before the lecturer reads it. The agent that wrote the slides does not check them; a separate one does, in three passes:

Correctness. Every statement, equation, number and reference is checked against the sources and the code output.
Typos and mechanics. Spelling, broken cross-references, mislabelled figures, equations that do not compile, slides that overflow.
Conformance to a written standard. The material is compared with a document that states how it should be written: the notation and house style in the instruction file, or a longer style guide stored as a workflow file (chapter 11). A guide to academic writing style, applied to papers and slides, is one example.

The third pass depends on the standard being written down. “Make it sound like me” gives the reviewer nothing to check against. A page of explicit rules does.
Keep the passes separate and ask for a list of findings with locations rather than a corrected file. You then decide which findings to accept, and the writing agent applies them. This can catch errors before the lecturer’s own reading, though it does not replace that reading.
Independent re-derivation in practice.

Session A writes questions and solutions.
Session B receives the questions only and writes its own solutions.
A script or a third session compares the two and lists every disagreement.
You resolve the disagreements. Agreement does not prove correctness, because both sessions can share a misconception.

References. Require a DOI or stable URL for every reference in material the agent writes, and have each one opened and checked. Do not accept a reference the agent cannot open. For the handful of papers a lecture rests on, check them yourself.
What cannot be delegated. Only you can judge whether an explanation is pitched at the right level, whether an example is fair to all students, and whether an argument is the one you want to teach. Read everything that goes to students at least once in full.
Before release.

Every number traced to code output
Code and notebooks run clean from top to bottom
Derivations and proofs independently re-derived
Every reference opened and confirmed
Notation checked against the instruction file
Independent review done: correctness, typos, conformance to the written standard
Read in full by the lecturer


In Claude Code. A subagent runs in its own context window and can be limited to read-only tools, which makes it a natural session B. Store it as a file in .claude/agents/ so the same checker is used every time (appendix).

title: 9  Student data, copyright and institutional policy
text:
Your own teaching material is yours to use with these tools; student work and third-party material are not. Most of the risk in using an agent for teaching comes from the second and third categories, and your university sets the rules for both. This chapter is general guidance and not legal advice.
Three kinds of material.








Material
Examples
Default position




Your own
Your notes, slides, questions, code
Free to use, subject to your employer’s IP policy


Student
Scripts, coursework, marks, emails, extenuating circumstances
Approved tools only, anonymised, and often not at all


Third party
Textbook chapters, publisher slides and test banks, journal articles, licensed datasets
Depends on the licence; ask the library



Student data. A script with a name or student number on it is personal data, and your university is responsible for how it is processed. Published UK policies are consistent on the default:

Liverpool lists uploading student work or personal data to public AI platforms as unacceptable without a data protection impact assessment or advice from the Data Protection Officer.
York requires explicit student permission before student work or details go into a generative AI tool.
Exeter notes that student work is by default the student’s intellectual property.

Anonymising helps but does not settle the matter: an essay can identify its author through its content, and the work still belongs to the student.
Approved tools and account types. Universities approve specific tools under specific contracts. A personal subscription to the same product is a different legal arrangement. The distinction that usually matters is whether the provider may train on what you send and how long it is kept.

In Claude Code. The data usage page distinguishes two cases. On personal plans (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra), data is used to train models when the account’s setting allows it, with retention of five years if allowed and 30 days if not. Under commercial terms (Team, Enterprise, API), prompts and code are not used for training unless the customer opts in, and standard retention is 30 days.
Session transcripts are also stored on your own machine, unencrypted, for 30 days by default, and transcripts of sessions started in the desktop app are kept with no age limit unless you set one. On a shared or unencrypted laptop, that is a further copy of anything you worked on.

Third-party teaching material. Putting a textbook chapter or a publisher’s test bank into a prompt is likely to count as copying for copyright purposes. Whether it is licensed depends on your university’s agreements.

The Copyright Licensing Agency added permission for copying into generative AI prompts to its business licences in May 2025. For the Higher Education licence, publishers were consulted in summer 2026 on adding equivalent permissions. Whether these are now in force was not confirmed at the time of writing, so ask your library.
Where such permissions exist in other CLA licences, they exclude training and require a tool whose terms do not allow training on prompts. A personal account with training switched on would not qualify.
Licensed datasets used in teaching have their own terms. Check before placing them in a folder the agent reads.

Output that reproduces a source. An exercise that closely follows a textbook problem may still infringe the publisher’s copyright, however it was produced. Ask the agent to write new questions to your specification, and do not ask it to rephrase existing ones.
Practical rules.

Keep student work out of the module folder unless you are using an approved tool for an approved purpose.
Keep third-party material in a separate subfolder of sources/ so it is easy to exclude.
Find your university’s list of approved AI tools and its staff guidance before the first use, and reread it each year.
If the guidance is silent on what you want to do, ask your Director of Education or the data protection team, and keep the answer.
crumbs: 9  Student data, copyright and institutional policy

title: 10  What to tell students
text:
Put a short AI statement in the module outline that says what students may do in each assessment and what you did in preparing the module. Permitted use differs across modules and assessments, so students need the rule for yours in writing.
What the statement should cover.

Per assessment: what use is permitted, in concrete terms. “You may use AI to debug code but not to write the interpretation” is usable. “Use AI responsibly” is not.
Disclosure: what students must declare and where, for example a short paragraph at the end of the submission naming the tool and what it was used for.
Responsibility: the student answers for everything submitted, including errors and invented references introduced by a tool.
Access: which tool the university provides at no cost, so that no assessment depends on a paid subscription.
Verification: that you may ask any student to explain their submission in person.
Your own use: how AI was used in preparing materials and, if at all, in marking and feedback.

Why include your own use. Guidance at several universities, including York and Exeter, asks staff to tell students when and how AI is used in marking and feedback. Extending that to teaching materials costs one sentence and makes it easier to ask the same openness of students.
Teach the checking as well as the rule. The first two Russell Group principles are about AI literacy and about equipping staff to support students’ use of AI. In a quantitative module, the most transferable habit is the one in chapter 5: a number is not trusted until the code that produced it has run. A short in-class demonstration of an agent producing a plausible but wrong answer makes the point concretely.
Keep it consistent across the programme. Agree a common format with colleagues so students see the same structure in every module, even where the permitted use differs. A shared scale (chapter 6) is one way to do this.
A template statement is in the appendix.

title: 11  Sharing workflows across a teaching team
text:
Once a workflow works for one module, write it down as a file the agent can follow, and share the file. A department then needs each workflow to be worked out only once for all its lecturers.
What is worth sharing.








Item
What it is
Who benefits




Module template
The empty folder layout and a skeleton instruction file (chapter 3)
Anyone starting or inheriting a module


Workflow files
Step-by-step instructions for a recurring task: new lecture, new problem set, annual update, stress test
Colleagues doing the same task


Checker
The independent checker from chapter 8, as a stored definition
Lecturers and teaching assistants


Statement template
The student-facing AI statement (chapter 10)
The whole programme



How to write a workflow file. Write it as you would brief a capable teaching assistant who has never seen the module:

What the task is and when to use it.
What inputs it needs and where they are.
The steps, in order, including the checks from chapter 8.
What the finished output looks like and where it goes.
What the agent must not do.

Test it by running it on a module other than the one it was written for. If it only works on your module, the module-specific parts belong in the instruction file.
Building a written standard for the reviewer. The third review pass in chapter 8 needs a document that says how your material should be written. It is built from your own work.

Collect examples. Five to ten pieces you consider your best: lecture notes, slides, problem sets, or papers if the standard is for research writing.
Have the agent extract the rules. Ask it to read them and list what is consistent: sentence and paragraph length, how a slide is structured, how a result is introduced, how equations are referenced, what is never done.
Edit the rules yourself. Delete what is accidental, correct what it misread, and add the rules you know you follow that the examples did not show.
Add pairs of examples. For each important rule, one passage that breaks it and the corrected version. The pair gives the reviewer something concrete to match.
Add a list of what to flag. The phrases and constructions you do not want, including those typical of machine-written text.
Say how to report. Findings as a list with location, the rule broken and a suggested fix. No rewriting.
Test it on old material. Run the reviewer on something you wrote before the standard existed, and on something an agent wrote. Adjust rules that produce false alarms.
Keep it current. Each time you correct the agent’s writing by hand, ask whether the correction is a rule. If so, add it.

One to three pages is enough. A standard built this way is specific to its author, so share the method and the template with colleagues rather than your own rules. A skeleton is in the appendix.
Where to keep shared files. Keep them in a departmental repository or shared drive, with one owner per file, and keep that location free of student data and of assessment content: workflows and templates only.
Teaching assistants. Give assistants the checker and the problem-set workflow but not the assessment folder. Agree in advance what they may use an agent for, and apply the same rule to all assistants on a module.
Handing a module over. The instruction file with its decisions log, the figure and solution scripts, and the workflow files together are the handover. A successor can ask the agent to explain how any week’s material was built and regenerate it.

In Claude Code. A workflow file is a skill: a folder containing a SKILL.md, stored in .claude/skills/<name>/ inside the module folder, or in ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ for personal use across modules. It runs when you type /<name>, or automatically when its description matches the task. Sharing is by committing .claude/skills/ to the shared repository.
The checker is a subagent definition in .claude/agents/. Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, so the same files are usable in other tools that support it.

title: 12  From assistant to agent: a worked example
text:
An assessment can be tested the way it will be used: one agent sets it, a second sits it, a third marks it, and the cycle repeats until the assessment holds up. This chapter builds that system. It is the one place in the handbook where the software decides its own next step.
Assistant or agent. In chapters 4 to 8 you set each task, approve the plan and fix the steps in advance. That is a supervised workflow. An agent, in the stricter sense, is given a goal and a stopping rule, and chooses its own actions from what it observes. The stress test in chapter 6 is the manual version of what follows.
Three roles, kept apart.









Role
Sees
Produces
Must not see




Setter
Learning outcomes, constraints, the examiner’s last report
The brief, data and rubric; a log of each change and its reason
The candidate’s working


Candidate
Only what a student receives
A complete submission
The rubric’s marking notes, the setter’s intentions, earlier rounds


Examiner
The submission and the rubric
A mark per criterion with a one-line justification
Who or what wrote the submission



The design depends on this separation: a candidate that has seen the marking notes, or an examiner that knows the submission is machine-written, tells you nothing.
One round.

The setter writes or revises the assessment and records what changed and why.
The candidate attempts it in a clean folder with only the student-facing files.
The examiner marks the attempt against the rubric, criterion by criterion.
The system checks the stopping rule.
If it is not met, the setter reads the examiner’s report, identifies the criteria the candidate passed most easily, and revises.




The assessment loop: three roles and one decision


Each pass runs left to right; an unmet stopping rule sends the examiner’s report back to the setter.
The stopping rule. Set it before the first round. For example: stop when the candidate’s mark falls below 50, or after five rounds, or when the setter cannot propose a change that respects the constraints. The third condition matters because some assessments cannot be made robust in their current format, and a report that says so is a useful result.
Constraints on the setter. Without them the loop converges on an assessment that defeats the candidate and is worthless for students. State them as rules the setter must satisfy in every round:

Every learning outcome assessed in the original is still assessed.
The format, weighting, word limit and time allowance are unchanged unless you allow otherwise.
A well-prepared student can complete it in the time given, using only what the module taught.
No change relies on obscurity, trick wording or information students cannot reasonably obtain.
Each change is logged with the criterion it targets.

The changes left open by these constraints mostly tie the task to something the candidate does not have: work done in class, data the student collects, a position defended orally, or a judgement that must be justified against material specific to the module.
What the report contains. The original and final versions side by side, the change log, the mark by criterion in every round, the final attempt in full, and the setter’s own assessment of which constraints came under strain.
What you still do.

Mark the final attempt yourself. The examiner is a language model, and chapter 7 documents how such marks are compressed towards the middle. Its marks steer the loop but are not evidence that the assessment is safe.
Judge validity. Read the final version as a student would. A harder assessment is not necessarily a better one.
Check the examiner once. Before trusting the loop, give the examiner two or three model answers you have written at known standards and see whether it ranks them correctly. Do not use real student scripts for this unless your university permits it (chapter 9).

Limits.

The candidate is not a student. It models a capable student using a current tool with little effort, which is the case the assessment has to withstand. It says nothing about how real students at different levels will perform.
The result is specific to the tool and the date. Record both and rerun each year.
A full run uses many times the computation of a single request. Start with a round limit of three.
This system has not been run on a live module. Treat the templates in the appendix as a starting design.

Other uses of the same three roles. For an invigilated exam, where AI use is not the concern, the loop still helps with quality: the candidate reports ambiguous wording and questions it could not finish in the time, and the examiner reports where the marking scheme gave no guidance. The setter revises for clarity instead of robustness.
By field. For empirical coursework, give the candidate the dataset and let it run code. For a theory problem set, the examiner needs full worked solutions in addition to final answers. For essay-based modules, expect the examiner’s marks to be least reliable, and rely more on your own marking of the final attempt.

In Claude Code. The candidate and examiner are subagents, each a file in .claude/agents/ with its own instructions and tool list. Setting omitClaudeMd: true starts a subagent without the module instruction file, which the candidate needs. The main session plays the setter and runs the loop from a skill.
A subagent in the same folder can still open files it is told not to. For a stricter test, copy the student-facing files to an empty folder outside the module and run the candidate there.

title: Templates
text:
Eight starting points to copy and edit. B, D, G and H use Claude Code’s file formats and are easily adapted; the others work with any tool. None has been tested on a live module, so run each on a small example first. Each is also a file in the templates/ folder of the repository.

A. Module instruction file
Save as MODULE.md, or as CLAUDE.md in Claude Code.
# ECN000 Module Title

## Module facts
Level 6, 15 credits, about 120 students. Prerequisites: ECN000, ECN000.

## Learning outcomes
1. ...
2. ...

## What students know
Assume: linear algebra to eigenvalues, OLS, basic Python (pandas, numpy).
Do not assume: maximum likelihood, matrix calculus, any R or Stata.

## Notation
Returns r_t, excess returns r^e_t. Vectors bold lower case, matrices bold upper case.
Estimators carry a hat. Follow the conventions of [textbook], chapters [x-y].

## Software
Python 3.12. Packages pinned in requirements.txt. No other packages.

## House style
British spelling. Lecture notes in LaTeX using lectures/template.tex.
One lecture is 100 minutes: at most 25 slides and two worked examples.

## Rules
- Never edit anything in sources/.
- Never supply a reference, fact or number that is not in sources/ or code output.
  If something is missing, stop and list it.
- Every number in a solution comes from a script that has been run.
- Compile or run every file before reporting it finished.
- No student work or personal data is stored in this folder.

## Decisions log
2026-11-26  Dropped the Kalman filter lecture; replaced by a second GMM lab.


B. Problem-set workflow
Save as .claude/skills/problem-set/SKILL.md. Run with /problem-set week05.
---
name: problem-set
description: Draft a problem set with verified solutions for one week of the module.
---

Write a problem set for $ARGUMENTS.

1. Read CLAUDE.md, the lecture notes for that week, and two past problem sets
   in problem-sets/ as the standard for style and difficulty.
2. Propose a one-page plan: each question, the outcome it tests, the expected
   time, and whether it is mechanical, applied or stretch. Wait for approval.
3. Write questions.tex, solutions.tex and solve.py in a new folder.
4. Run solve.py. Take every number in solutions.tex from its output.
5. For derivations, verify each final expression symbolically or numerically.
6. Compile both .tex files and fix any errors.
7. Report: what was produced, what was verified and how, and anything you
   could not verify.

Do not reuse or paraphrase questions from textbooks in sources/.


C. Marking notes to feedback
Use only with a tool your university has approved for student work (chapter 9).
Below are my marking notes for one anonymised script and the rubric.
I have already set the mark; do not suggest or comment on a mark.

Write feedback of about 150 words:
- one sentence on what the script did well, taken from my notes;
- the two most important improvements, each tied to a rubric criterion;
- one concrete step for the next assessment.

Use only what is in my notes. Do not add observations of your own.

Rubric: [paste]
Notes: [paste]


D. Independent checker
Save as .claude/agents/checker.md.
---
name: checker
description: Independently solves a problem set from the questions alone and reports disagreements with the official solutions. Use before any solutions are released.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are checking a problem set for a university module.

1. Read the questions file only. Do not open the solutions yet.
2. Solve every question yourself. You cannot run code: where a number requires
   computation, write the code in your report and mark the number as unconfirmed.
3. Only then read the official solutions.
4. For each question report: agree, or disagree with both answers and the
   likely source of the difference.
5. Separately list any question that is ambiguous, answerable without the
   intended method, or harder than its stated level.

You do not edit files or run code. You report.


E. Student-facing AI statement
Use of AI tools in ECN000

Problem sets (not assessed): any use is permitted. You will learn more by
attempting each question before asking a tool.

Coursework (40%): you may use AI tools to debug code and to check grammar.
You may not use them to write the interpretation of results or the conclusion.
Add a short declaration at the end of your submission naming any tool used
and what you used it for. You are responsible for everything you submit,
including errors and references introduced by a tool. You may be asked to
explain your submission in person.

Exam (60%): invigilated, no AI tools.

The university provides [tool] to all students at no cost. No assessment in
this module requires a paid subscription.

How AI was used in preparing this module: lecture notes and problem sets were
drafted with an AI coding agent from my own notes and checked by me. All
marks are set by the teaching team. [State any use in feedback.]


F. Assessment stress test

Fresh session in an empty folder, no module files
Agent given only what a student receives
One-pass attempt saved
Attempt with one round of student-style follow-up saved
Both marked against the rubric, blind where possible
Criteria where marks were lost recorded
Decision recorded: keep, modify, or move to supervised conditions
Date and tool version recorded for next year’s comparison



G. A written standard as a skill
Save as .claude/skills/lecture-style/SKILL.md, with more pairs of examples in examples.md in the same folder (a placeholder version is in the repository’s templates/ folder). The rules shown are placeholders: replace them with your own (chapter 11).
---
name: lecture-style
description: House style for lecture notes and slides in my modules. Use when writing or reviewing any teaching material.
---

## Rules
1. One idea per slide. A slide has a title that states the point, not the topic.
2. Paragraphs in notes are at most four sentences.
3. Every equation that is used later is numbered; no others are.
4. A new symbol is defined in the sentence where it first appears.
5. Each result is followed by one sentence of interpretation in plain words.
6. Worked examples use real data and state the source and sample period.

## Do not
- Open a section by announcing what it will do.
- Use rhetorical questions as slide titles.
- Use: "it is important to note", "delve", "crucial", "in today's world".

## Examples
Breaks rule 1:   title "Fama-MacBeth regressions"
Corrected:       title "Fama-MacBeth: estimate the price of risk period by period"
(more pairs in examples.md)

## When reviewing
Do not rewrite. Report each finding as:
  file and location | rule number | what is wrong | suggested fix
Finish with a count of findings per rule.


H. Assessment loop: setter, candidate, examiner
Three files for the system in chapter 12. Untested: run it first on a short problem set with a round limit of two.
Save as .claude/agents/candidate.md:
---
name: candidate
description: Attempts an assessment exactly as a student would, from the student-facing files only.
omitClaudeMd: true
---

You are a student taking this module. You have been given a folder containing
the assessment brief and any data. Read only the files in that folder.

Complete the assessment in full and save your submission in the folder.
Work as a capable student would with the tools available: write and run code
where needed, and check your own work once before submitting.

Do not look for a rubric, marking notes or solutions. Do not ask questions.
When finished, list any wording you found ambiguous.
Save as .claude/agents/examiner.md:
---
name: examiner
description: Marks one anonymous submission against a rubric, criterion by criterion.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are marking one anonymous submission. You are given the submission and
the rubric. Assume nothing about who wrote it.

For each criterion give: a mark, the band, and one sentence quoting or
pointing to the evidence in the submission. You cannot run code: check each
reported number against the code output saved in the submission, list any
number you cannot confirm this way, and do not award marks for it.

Then give the total, and list the two criteria on which the submission was
strongest. Report any place where the rubric gave you no guidance.
You do not edit files or run code.
Save as .claude/skills/assessment-loop/SKILL.md. Run with /assessment-loop assessment/coursework1.
---
name: assessment-loop
description: Iteratively tests and revises an assessment using a candidate and an examiner subagent.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

You are the setter for the assessment in $ARGUMENTS.

Settings (edit before running):
  stop when the candidate's total is below 50, or after 3 rounds,
  or when no revision satisfies the constraints.

Constraints on every revision:
  - every learning outcome in CLAUDE.md that the original assessed is still assessed
  - format, weighting, word limit and time allowance unchanged
  - a well-prepared student can complete it using only what the module taught
  - no trick wording and no reliance on information students cannot obtain

Each round:
  1. Copy the student-facing files to rounds/roundN/student/.
  2. Use the candidate subagent on that folder only.
  3. Use the examiner subagent on the submission and the rubric.
  4. Save the examiner's report to rounds/roundN/report.md.
  5. Check the stopping rule. If met, go to the final report.
  6. Identify the criteria passed most easily. Propose one or two revisions
     that satisfy every constraint. Record each in changes.md with the
     criterion it targets and the reason. Apply them to a new version.

Final report (report.md): original and final versions, the change log,
marks by criterion for every round, the final attempt in full, and which
constraints came under strain. State plainly if the format could not be
made robust.

Never edit the original assessment files. Work on copies.
